## What Section 7 Actually Requires

- **Each side has to defend and pay for the other** when an outside person or company sues the other side because of something the first side did wrong — specifically, breaking a promise in the contract, being extremely careless or acting on purpose to cause harm, or delivering something that steals or copies someone else's intellectual property.

- **The IP-infringement protection has three carve-outs.** You are NOT protected if the problem was caused by (i) changes you made to what was delivered, (ii) combining what was delivered with other stuff that wasn't supplied by the other party (and the problem only happened because of that mix), or (iii) using what was delivered in a way the contract doesn't allow.

- **If you get sued, you must (a) tell the other party in writing right away, (b) hand them the steering wheel to defend and settle the case, and (c) cooperate reasonably (they pay your out-of-pocket costs for helping).** If you're late to notify them, they can only reduce their obligation to the extent the delay actually hurt their ability to defend — not use it as a free pass.

- **The party running the defense cannot settle in a way that admits you did something wrong or forces you to do something (like stop selling a product) without your written OK** — and you can't unreasonably say no.

- **Neither side can be sued for "soft" damages** like lost profits, lost revenue, lost future business, reputation damage, or lost data — even if the other side warned them these losses could happen.

- **There is a hard dollar cap on total liability**: whichever is BIGGER of (A) the fees the customer paid or owed the provider in the 12 months before the problem started, or (B) $100,000.

- **Four things break through both the "no soft damages" rule AND the dollar cap** — meaning unlimited exposure: (1) the indemnification promises in 7.1, (2) breaking the confidentiality section (Section 9), (3) gross negligence or willful misconduct, and (4) infringing the other party's IP.

- **Bottom line for you as the business owner**: for ordinary mistakes and disputes, your worst-case bill is the 12-month fees or $100k (whichever is greater). But if you seriously mess up (grossly negligent, deliberate wrongdoing, leaking their secrets, stealing their IP, or triggering an indemnity claim), the cap disappears and you're exposed to the full amount.

## Key Terms Glossary

- **Indemnify / hold harmless** — A promise to step in and pay for the other side's legal problems (defense costs, settlements, judgments) so they don't end up out of pocket.

- **Third-party claim** — A lawsuit, demand, or legal action brought by someone who is NOT you and NOT the other party to the contract (like a customer, competitor, or regulator suing one of you).

- **Gross negligence vs. willful misconduct** — Gross negligence is being so careless it goes way beyond a normal mistake (reckless disregard); willful misconduct is knowing what you're doing is wrong and doing it anyway on purpose.

- **Intellectual property infringement or misappropriation** — Using, copying, or delivering something that violates someone else's patent, copyright, trademark, or trade secret rights without permission.

- **Consequential / incidental / punitive damages** — "Ripple effect" losses (like lost profits from a shutdown), side costs tied to the main problem (like renting a replacement), and extra punishment money a court adds to make an example of the wrongdoer — all beyond the direct, obvious cost of the harm itself.

- **Cap on liability** — A pre-agreed ceiling on the maximum dollar amount one side can ever be forced to pay the other, no matter how bad the damage gets.

- **Sole control of the defense** — The indemnifying party gets to fully run the lawsuit — pick the lawyers, decide the strategy, and negotiate the settlement — instead of the party being sued.

- **Materially prejudiced** — Meaningfully hurt in a real, significant way (not just a minor inconvenience) — here, it means the late notice actually damaged the defender's ability to fight the case.
